questions.q: In an if/elif/else chain, how many branches actually run?
options: Only the first one whose condition is True — the rest are skipped entirely
Every branch always runs, regardless of the condition
Only the else branch ever runs
All branches run in reverse order
questions.explain: Python checks conditions top to bottom and stops at the first True one.

questions.q: What is the difference between = and == in Python?
options: = assigns a value to a variable; == compares two values for equality
They are interchangeable and mean the same thing
= is used only for numbers; == is used only for strings
== assigns a value; = compares two values
questions.explain: Mixing these up is one of the most common early Python mistakes.

questions.q: What does the 'and' operator require to evaluate to True?
options: Both sides of the condition must be True
Only one side needs to be True
Neither side can be True
and always evaluates to True regardless of the operands
questions.explain: and is stricter than or — every combined condition must hold.

questions.q: What does 'not' do to a condition?
options: Flips its truth value entirely — True becomes False and vice versa
Combines two conditions into one
Only works on numeric values
Deletes the condition from the program
questions.explain: not (fare_amount > 0) is true exactly when fare_amount > 0 is false.

questions.q: In the is_valid_trip example, what causes it to return False?
options: If fare_amount, passenger_count, or trip_distance is zero or negative
Only if all three values are negative simultaneously
It always returns False regardless of input
Only if passenger_count is exactly 1
questions.explain: Each condition checks one business rule in sequence, returning False as soon as any rule fails.
